We'll roll a custom exponential-backoff scheduler inline in each worker

questions.question:
D6 — When webhooks gain retries, what delivery guarantee do customers get?
Project/branch/task: main — PLAN.md "Add background job retry framework", Tests section (PLAN.md:16-18) rewriting processWebhookJob().
ELI10: Today a webhook is sent once; if it fails, it's gone ("at-most-once"). The moment you add retries, a customer's server can receive the same event twice, because "the request timed out" and "the request failed" look identical to us but the customer may have processed it. That is "at-least-once," and it is what Stripe, GitHub and Shopify all do: they include an idempotency key (a stable event id) so the customer can ignore duplicates. The plan rewrites the webhook flow under the retry framework without saying which promise customers get. Silently switching is the one option that is wrong.
Stakes if we pick wrong: a customer double-fulfills an order on a duplicate event, or, if we keep at-most-once by accident, a transient 5xx drops a payment notification with no retry and no record.
Recommendation: A because retrying is why this flow is being touched, and at-least-once plus an idempotency key is the industry-standard, documented contract; B is the right pick only if customers cannot dedupe.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: retries with a documented dedupe key vs. no retries for webhooks at all; the hidden third option (retry silently under an at-most-once promise) is off the table.

options.label: At-least-once + idempotency key (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Transient customer-side failures get retried on the shared curve; deliveries stop vanishing on a single 5xx. ✅ A stable per-event idempotency key header lets consumers dedupe, matching the contract every major webhook provider documents. ❌ Customer-visible contract change: needs a docs/changelog note, and consumers who never deduped may see duplicates until they do (human: ~2 days incl. docs / CC: ~30 min).

options.label: Keep at-most-once: webhook worker opts out
options.description: ✅ Zero change to what customers observe; the existing promise is preserved exactly. ✅ Simplest regression test: assert the webhook worker registers with maxAttempts=1. ❌ Webhooks get none of the reliability this whole plan is for; a transient 5xx still loses the event, and terminal handling (R7) becomes the only safety net.

questions.question:
D7 — Add jitter to the backoff curve?
Project/branch/task: main — PLAN.md "Add background job retry framework", the custom backoff function approved in D4.
ELI10: Exponential backoff means "wait 1s, then 2s, then 4s." If a shared dependency (database, third-party API) blips and 2,000 jobs fail in the same second, plain exponential backoff retries all 2,000 at exactly the same instant, three times in a row, recreating the spike that caused the failure. Jitter randomizes each job's wait inside the window (0 to the computed delay), so the 2,000 retries spread out instead of arriving as a wall. It is one multiply by a random number.
Stakes if we pick wrong: without jitter, the retry framework can turn a 5-second blip into a self-inflicted outage; with it, the same blip drains smoothly.
Recommendation: A because it is a one-line change to the backoff function and it is the single most-cited retry pitfall in current guidance.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10
Net: one random multiply vs. synchronized retry storms under exactly the conditions retries exist for.

options.label: Full jitter (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Spreads simultaneous retries across the whole window so a dependency recovering from an outage is not re-hammered in lockstep. ✅ One line in the shared backoff function; unit test asserts delay stays within [0, cap] for every attempt (CC: ~2 min). ❌ Delays are non-deterministic, so tests must seed or stub the RNG and dashboards see a range rather than a fixed schedule.

options.label: Deterministic exponential, no jitter
options.description: ✅ Exact, predictable retry times; easy to reason about in logs and tests. ✅ Nothing to stub or seed in unit tests. ❌ Every job that failed together retries together, so a shared-dependency blip becomes a repeating spike at 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s.

questions.question:
D8 — Cap the retries, and where do exhausted jobs go?
Project/branch/task: main — PLAN.md "Add background job retry framework", shared retryPolicy defaults (D4/D5).
ELI10: Some jobs will never succeed: a malformed payload, a deleted customer, a webhook URL that now 404s. Without a maximum, those jobs retry forever, quietly eating worker time and log volume. A cap (say 8 attempts over ~15 minutes with jitter) stops them, but then they have to go somewhere. A "dead set" is the library's parking lot for exhausted jobs: you can list them, inspect the error, and replay them after a fix. An alert on that parking lot filling up is how a tired human at 3am finds out a downstream is broken.
Stakes if we pick wrong: no cap means zombie jobs and a queue that never drains; cap-and-log-only means exhausted jobs are gone the moment logs rotate and there's nothing to replay.
Recommendation: A because the dead set already exists in the library, the alert is one metric threshold, and "exhausted jobs are visible and replayable" is the whole point of a retry framework you can operate.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10, C=2/10
Net: bounded retries with a replayable parking lot and a pager signal vs. exhausted jobs that either never stop or silently disappear. Concrete defaults proposed: maxAttempts=8, base=1s, cap=15min; per-worker overrides allowed.

options.label: Cap + dead set + alert (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Exhausted jobs land in the library's dead/failed set with the last error, so they can be inspected and replayed after a fix. ✅ One structured `job.exhausted` log line plus an alert on dead-set growth means a broken downstream pages someone instead of hiding (human: ~1 day / CC: ~15 min). ❌ Needs an alert threshold and an owner for the dead set; an unwatched dead set is a slower version of log-only.

options.label: Cap + log only
options.description: ✅ Stops infinite retries with the least new surface: one log line when attempts run out. ✅ No alert wiring or dead-set ownership to set up. ❌ Exhausted jobs are unrecoverable once logs rotate; a downstream outage that kills 500 jobs leaves nothing to replay and nobody is paged.

options.label: No cap, retry until success
options.description: ✅ Nothing is ever dropped; a fixed downstream eventually drains everything. ✅ No terminal handling to design at all. ❌ Permanently-bad jobs (deleted customer, 404 webhook URL) retry forever, consuming workers and log volume with zero signal that anything is wrong.

questions.question:
D9 — Retry every failure, or only the transient ones?
Project/branch/task: main — PLAN.md "Add background job retry framework", shared retryPolicy module (D5) error handling.
ELI10: Failures come in two kinds. Transient: the network dropped, the downstream timed out, it answered 503 or 429 ("slow down"). Those get better if you wait. Permanent: the webhook URL returns 404, the payload fails validation, the customer was deleted. Those never get better. The plan retries everything the same way, so a permanent failure burns 8 attempts over 15 minutes before it finally lands in the dead set where someone can see it. A small `isRetryable(err)` check in the shared module sends permanent failures straight to the dead set on attempt one.
Stakes if we pick wrong: retry-everything means a bad deploy that breaks validation for all jobs shows up in the dead-set alert 15 minutes late and after 8x the load; misclassifying a transient error as permanent means one blip kills a job that would have succeeded on the next try.
Recommendation: A because the classification is ~15 lines, it makes the dead-set alert fire immediately for real bugs, and the conservative default (unknown error = retry) protects against misclassification.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10
Net: a small classifier that makes permanent failures visible in seconds vs. uniform retries that delay every real bug signal by the full curve.

options.label: Classify: retry transient, dead-letter permanent (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Permanent failures (404, 4xx except 408/429, validation, explicit NonRetryableError) hit the dead set and alert on attempt one instead of 15 minutes later. ✅ Default for unknown errors is retry, so misclassification fails safe; unit tests cover each class (human: ~half day / CC: ~10 min). ❌ One more concept in the module, and the HTTP-status mapping needs a home for per-worker exceptions (e.g. a partner API that returns 400 for rate limits).

options.label: Retry everything up to the cap
options.description: ✅ Simplest possible rule; no classifier to maintain or get wrong. ✅ A job that fails for a surprising-but-transient reason still gets its full 8 attempts. ❌ A permanent failure retries 8 times over 15 minutes, so a real bug reaches the dead-set alert late and with 8x the load, and a 404 webhook URL gets hammered pointlessly.

questions.question:
D10 — How do we lock in the webhook regression contract?
Project/branch/task: main — PLAN.md "Add background job retry framework", processWebhookJob() rewrite (PLAN.md:16-18).
ELI10: The webhook code is being rewritten, and today nothing proves it still does what it did. What must stay the same: on a good first try, exactly one POST goes out, and the body, signature header and content-type are byte-for-byte what customers get today. What changes on purpose (D6/D8/D9): a 503 gets retried with the same Idempotency-Key and identical body; a 404 is sent once and parked; 8 failures park the job. Unit tests with stubs are cheap and great for the byte-level details, but the retry behavior itself happens inside the job library (attempt counting, requeue), and a stub of the library is exactly the thing that hides a misconfigured hook. One test through the real queue against a tiny local HTTP receiver catches that.
Stakes if we pick wrong: a subtle header or body change ships to every webhook customer, or the retry hook is wired wrong and no webhook ever retries in production while all the unit tests pass.
Recommendation: C because the unit suite enumerates the cheap edge cases and the single integration test proves the library actually drives the retries; with CC the extra test is minutes.
Completeness: A=7/10, B=6/10, C=10/10
Net: stubs prove the bytes, the real queue proves the retries; only C proves both.

options.description: ✅ Unit tests pin body/signature/headers with a golden snapshot of today's output and cover every error class; the integration test proves 200 = 1 POST, 503→200 = 2 POSTs same key, 404 = 1 POST then dead set. ✅ Catches the failure stubs cannot: a retry hook registered wrong so nothing ever retries (human: ~2 days / CC: ~30 min). ❌ Integration test needs a local queue backend in CI and an in-process HTTP receiver; slower than unit tests alone.

options.label: Unit tests with stubs
options.description: ✅ Fast, deterministic, and ideal for byte-level payload and header assertions plus every isRetryable branch. ✅ No queue backend needed in CI (human: ~1 day / CC: ~15 min). ❌ Stubs the library boundary where the retry actually happens, so a misregistered hook or wrong attempt indexing passes green and fails in prod.

options.label: One integration test through the real queue
options.description: ✅ Exercises the true path: enqueue → library retry → worker → HTTP receiver, including attempt counting. ✅ Directly demonstrates the customer-visible contract end to end. ❌ Slow and coarse: enumerating every error class and edge (overflow, rng bounds, header set) through a real queue is impractical, so most branches stay untested.

questions.question:
D11 — Reuse the dependency graph across retries?
Project/branch/task: main — PLAN.md "Add background job retry framework", Performance section (PLAN.md:21-23).
ELI10: Each attempt currently re-reads the whole job payload from the database and rebuilds a dependency graph from it. The graph doesn't change between attempts (same job, same payload), so attempts 2 through 8 redo work attempt 1 already did, and they do it while the system is already struggling (that's why the job is retrying). Because the library now schedules retries (D4), the retry may run on a different worker process, so keeping the graph in memory won't help; it has to be stored with the job. Storing it once, tagged with a hash of the payload, means every retry reuses it and, as a bonus, always sees the same graph attempt 1 saw.
Stakes if we pick wrong: leave it and a struggling dependency eats up to 8x the read/compute load per failing job; persist it wrong (no payload hash) and a retry could use a stale graph after a payload edit.
Recommendation: A because it is ~30 lines (serialize on attempt 1, check hash on retry), it removes load from the worst possible moment, and it makes retries deterministic.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=5/10, C=4/10
Net: a small persisted cache with a hash guard vs. redoing attempt 1's work up to 7 more times under load.

options.label: Persist graph in job data on first attempt (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Retries skip the payload re-fetch and graph walk; load on a struggling dependency drops to one compute per job instead of up to eight. ✅ Payload hash guard means a changed payload recomputes, and retries otherwise see exactly attempt 1's graph (deterministic) (human: ~1 day / CC: ~15 min). ❌ Serialized graph adds bytes to each job record; needs a unit test for hash-match reuse and hash-mismatch recompute.

options.label: In-process memo keyed by job id
options.description: ✅ Trivial to write: a Map in the worker module, no serialization. ✅ Helps when the retry happens to land on the same warm process. ❌ The library may hand the retry to any worker, and a restart wipes the memo, so in practice most retries still recompute; also an unbounded Map is a slow memory leak.

options.label: Recompute every attempt (as planned)
options.description: ✅ No new persisted state or cache invalidation to reason about. ✅ Bounded by the 8-attempt cap (D8), so worst case is 8x per failing job, not unbounded. ❌ Redundant DB read + graph walk on every retry, concentrated exactly when a dependency is unhealthy; retries can compute a different graph than attempt 1 if the payload changed.

answers.D11 \u2014 Reuse the dependency graph ac: Persist graph in job data on first attempt (recommended)

questions.question:
D12 — TODO: tune the dead-set alert threshold from production data?
Project/branch/task: main — PLAN.md "Add background job retry framework"; follow-up to D8 (cap + dead set + alert).
ELI10: D8 adds an alert when the dead set grows. At implementation we have to pick a number (say "more than 20 exhausted jobs in 10 minutes") with no production data behind it. Too low and it pages on noise; too high and a real outage sits unnoticed. The right number only shows up after a couple of weeks of real traffic.
What: after ~2 weeks in production, review dead-set growth per worker and set per-worker alert thresholds; record the baseline in the runbook.
Why: a guessed threshold is either noisy or blind; a measured one is neither.
Pros: the alert becomes trustworthy, so on-call actually reacts to it.
Cons: a calendar reminder someone has to honor; needs whoever owns on-call to spend ~1 hour.
Context: threshold and owner are set in the D8 implementation; this TODO revisits them with data. Depends on: the retry framework shipping and the dead-set metric existing.
Recommendation: A because the initial threshold is a guess by construction and the review is cheap.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: a dated follow-up vs. living with a guessed pager threshold.

D3 — Let gstack search learnings from your other projects on this machine?

ELI10: gstack records small lessons per project (pitfalls, patterns). Cross-project mode lets this review also read lessons saved from your other repos on this machine, so a retry-scheduler footgun learned elsewhere shows up here. Everything stays local; nothing leaves the machine.

questions.question:
D4 — Who owns retry scheduling: the job library's hooks, or a custom scheduler inlined in each worker?
Project/branch/task: main branch, "Plan: Add background job retry framework" (PLAN.md:6-8).
ELI10: The plan rebuilds something the job library already does: deciding when a failed job runs again. The plan's reason is "full control over the curve", but every mainstream job library lets you plug in your own delay function while it still owns the hard part: remembering the pending retry so it survives a worker crash or deploy. An in-process scheduler forgets every pending retry the moment the worker restarts.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Custom inline scheduling means retries silently vanish on every deploy, plus five copies of scheduler code to keep correct. Library hooks mean one shared backoff function and persisted retry state, at the cost of learning the hook API.
Recommendation: A because it keeps full control over the curve (one function you own) while the library keeps retry state durable. [Layer 1] reuse; the plan already names the built-in it is avoiding.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=5/10, C=n/a (investigation, no change)
Net: owning one backoff function vs. owning a scheduler and its crash-persistence problem in five places. (human: A ~1 day / CC: ~20 min; B ~3 days / CC: ~1 hr plus persistence work)

options.label: Library hooks + shared backoff (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Retry state lives in the queue, so pending retries survive worker restarts and deploys. ✅ Full curve control via one shared computeBackoff(attempt) function; nothing to re-implement. ❌ Bound to the library's hook signature; any curve feature it cannot express needs a workaround.

options.label: Custom inline scheduler (as planned)
options.description: ✅ No dependency on the library's hook API or its release cadence. ✅ Arbitrary scheduling logic possible, including cross-job coordination. ❌ Pending retries are lost on worker restart unless you also build persistence; five copies of scheduler code to keep correct.

options.label: Investigate library hooks first
options.description: ✅ Confirms the actual hook signature and whether it accepts a per-attempt delay function before committing. ✅ Cheap: read the library docs and one existing worker (CC: ~5 min). ❌ Delays the decision; leaves R1 pending and blocks the dependent dedup choice.

questions.question:
D5 — What delivery guarantee do webhooks have once they can retry?
Project/branch/task: main branch, "Plan: Add background job retry framework" (PLAN.md:16-18), Architecture review.
ELI10: Today a webhook is sent at most once: if it fails, it is gone, but a receiver never sees it twice. The moment you retry, a webhook whose response timed out may have actually arrived, so the retry delivers it again. That is a contract change for every customer receiving webhooks, and the plan does not say so. Receivers can only dedupe if every delivery carries a stable id.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Silent duplicates mean customers get double charges, double emails, or double state changes with no way to detect it. Preserving at-most-once means most real failures (timeouts, 5xx) can never be retried, which is most of the value.
Recommendation: A because at-least-once plus a stable idempotency key is the industry-standard webhook contract (Stripe, GitHub, Shopify all do this) and it makes retries safe for receivers.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10, C=2/10
Net: safe retries with a documented receiver contract vs. no duplicates but almost no retries vs. duplicates with no warning. (human: A ~1 day / CC: ~20 min; B ~half day / CC: ~15 min)

options.label: At-least-once + idempotency key (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Every failure class becomes retryable; receivers dedupe on a stable event/delivery id header. ✅ Matches what every major webhook provider documents, so receivers already expect it. ❌ Contract change: must be documented for receivers and needs a stable id persisted with the job across attempts.

options.label: Preserve at-most-once
options.description: ✅ No receiver ever sees a duplicate; existing receiver code needs no change. ✅ Still safe to retry provable pre-send failures like connection refused or DNS errors. ❌ Timeouts and 5xx responses cannot be retried, so most real-world webhook failures stay unrecovered.

options.label: Keep plan as written (no contract)
options.description: ✅ Zero extra work in this change; smallest diff. ✅ Behavior matches whatever the rewrite happens to do. ❌ Duplicates reach receivers with no id to dedupe on and no documentation that the guarantee changed.

questions.question:
D6.1 — How many times does a job retry, and what happens after the last failure?
Project/branch/task: main branch, "Plan: Add background job retry framework"; Architecture review, retry policy bounds (the plan states none).
ELI10: "Exponential backoff" says how long to wait between tries, not when to stop. Without a max, a job hitting a permanently dead endpoint retries forever and you never find out. With a max you also have to decide where the job goes after its final failure: parked somewhere you can inspect and replay (dead-letter), or just marked failed in a log line.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Unbounded means zombie jobs eating queue capacity indefinitely. Bounded with log-only means the final error scrolls past at 3am and the payload is gone; nobody can replay it.
Recommendation: A because dead-letter is the difference between "we lost 40 webhooks last night" and "we replayed 40 webhooks this morning". Most job libraries already ship a failed/dead set, so it is configuration, not code.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10, C=2/10
Net: replayable failures vs. a log line vs. jobs that never stop. (human: A ~half day / CC: ~10 min; B ~2 hrs / CC: ~5 min)

options.label: Bounded + dead-letter (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Final failures are parked with payload and last error; an operator can inspect and replay them. ✅ Per-job-type max attempts (default 8) plus an alert-level log on terminal failure makes silent loss impossible. ❌ Someone has to own the dead-letter set; unwatched it becomes a graveyard.

options.label: Bounded + fail and log only
options.description: ✅ Simplest bounded policy; a max-attempts number and a log line, nothing to operate. ✅ Queue capacity is protected exactly as in A. ❌ After the final failure the payload is gone; recovery means re-creating the job by hand from logs.

options.label: Unbounded retries
options.description: ✅ No job is ever declared dead; transient outages of any length eventually recover. ✅ Zero policy decisions to make per job type. ❌ Permanently failing jobs retry forever, consuming queue slots and hammering dead endpoints with no signal to anyone.

questions.question:
D6.2 — Should the backoff delay have a maximum, or grow without limit?
Project/branch/task: main branch, "Plan: Add background job retry framework"; Architecture review, retry policy bounds. Max attempts (default 8) and dead-letter are already approved (D6.1); this decides only the per-attempt wait.
ELI10: Exponential backoff doubles the wait each time: 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s... By attempt 12 that is over an hour; by attempt 20 it is 12 days. A cap says "never wait more than X", so late retries keep a sane cadence instead of drifting into next week. With 8 attempts the difference is small, but a per-job-type override to 15 or 20 attempts makes it enormous.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Uncapped means a job type configured for more attempts silently waits days between tries. Capped costs one min() call.
Recommendation: A because a cap is one line, makes the total retry window predictable, and every production backoff implementation (AWS SDK, gRPC, Google's guidance) caps.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10
Net: a predictable retry window vs. one fewer parameter. (human: ~1 hr / CC: ~2 min either way)

options.label: Cap at per-job-type max (recommended)
options.description: ✅ delay = min(base * 2^attempt, maxDelay); default maxDelay 1 hour, overridable per worker. ✅ Total retry window stays predictable even when a job type raises its attempt count. ❌ One more parameter to document and test alongside base and maxAttempts.

options.label: No cap, pure exponential
options.description: ✅ Simplest formula; base and attempt count fully determine the curve. ✅ Long tails naturally back off hard from a struggling downstream. ❌ Job types with higher attempt counts wait hours then days between tries with no ceiling.

questions.question:
D6.3 — Randomize each retry delay (jitter), or keep delays deterministic?
Project/branch/task: main branch, "Plan: Add background job retry framework"; Architecture review, last retry-policy bound. Attempts, dead-letter and cap are approved (D6.1, D6.2); this decides only whether delays are randomized.
ELI10: When a downstream service blips, hundreds of jobs fail in the same second. Without jitter they all retry in the same second too, then the same second again: a thundering herd that keeps knocking the service over. Jitter spreads each retry randomly across its window so the herd arrives as a trickle. The cost is that tests need an injectable random source to stay deterministic.
Stakes if we pick wrong: No jitter means your own retries can prolong the outage they are recovering from. Jitter without an injectable RNG means flaky tests.
Recommendation: A because full jitter (random between 0 and the capped delay) is the documented best practice from AWS's backoff analysis and costs one random() call plus an injected RNG parameter.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10
Net: outage-safe retry spreading vs. simpler, exactly predictable delays. (human: ~2 hrs / CC: ~3 min either way)

options.label: Full jitter, injectable RNG (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Correlated failures spread across the retry window instead of retrying in lockstep. ✅ Injected RNG keeps computeBackoff tests exact (seeded) and lets a bounds test assert 0 <= delay <= cap. ❌ Individual retry times are no longer predictable by hand from the attempt number.

options.label: Deterministic, no jitter
options.description: ✅ Delay is a pure function of attempt number; trivially testable and easy to reason about in logs. ✅ No RNG parameter to thread through. ❌ Every job that failed together retries together, so a recovering downstream gets hit by the whole herd at once.

questions.question:
D7 — Extract the retry envelope into one shared module now, or keep five copy-pasted copies and refactor later?
Project/branch/task: main branch, "Plan: Add background job retry framework" (PLAN.md:11-13), Code Quality review.
ELI10: The plan says the same block of code (compute delay, log the attempt, dispatch) will be pasted into five worker files and cleaned up "later". Every bound we just approved (cap, jitter, max attempts, dead-letter) would then be implemented five times, and every future fix has to land in five places or the workers silently drift apart. With the library-hook approach from D4, the shared version is small: one module with computeBackoff, logAttempt and a wrapper that registers the hook; each worker becomes a one-line policy declaration.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Five copies means the first bug fix ships to four workers and misses the fifth. Extracting now costs about the same as pasting it once, since there is only one body to write.
Recommendation: A because DRY here is not premature abstraction: the five call sites already exist, the body is identical by the plan's own words, and "later" refactors of retry code rarely happen because the code appears to work.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=4/10
Net: one place to get retries right vs. five places to get them wrong. (human: A ~1 day / CC: ~15 min; B ~1 day now plus a refactor ticket nobody picks up)

options.label: Extract shared retry module now (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Cap, jitter, max attempts, dead-letter, logging land once; five workers declare {maxAttempts, base, maxDelay} and nothing else. ✅ One test suite proves the envelope; per-worker tests only check the hook is wired and the policy values. ❌ Introduces one new module the team must learn; a worker with a truly unique need has to extend it rather than fork it.

options.label: Keep 5 copies, refactor later
options.description: ✅ Each worker is self-contained; you can read one file and see everything it does. ✅ No new shared abstraction to design under time pressure. ❌ Every approved bound is written and tested five times; drift between copies is invisible until a production incident shows one worker retrying differently.

questions.question:
D8 — Should every failure retry, or should permanent failures skip straight to dead-letter?
Project/branch/task: main branch, "Plan: Add background job retry framework"; Code Quality review, error-handling gap. The plan never says which errors retry.
ELI10: Some failures fix themselves if you wait: a timeout, a 503, a dropped connection. Others never will: a webhook URL returning 404, a payload that fails validation, a bug in the job. Retrying a permanent failure eight times over four hours does nothing except delay the moment someone finds out and burn queue capacity. A small classifier (network/timeout/5xx/429 retry; 4xx/validation/explicit NonRetryableError go terminal) sends permanent failures to dead-letter on the first attempt.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Retry-everything hides bugs for hours and hammers customers' dead webhook endpoints with 8 identical requests. Over-aggressive classification can mark a recoverable error terminal; that is why 408/425/429 stay retryable.
Recommendation: A because the taxonomy is small, well-known (it mirrors what Stripe and Sidekiq do), and it is the only way dead-letter surfaces real bugs quickly.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=5/10
Net: fast surfacing of real failures vs. simpler rule that delays every permanent failure by the full retry window. (human: A ~half day / CC: ~10 min)

options.label: Classify retryable vs permanent (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Permanent failures (4xx except 408/425/429, validation, NonRetryableError) dead-letter on attempt 1 with the real error attached. ✅ Retryable set is explicit and tested: network errors, timeouts, 5xx, 408/425/429. ❌ A misclassified error class can go terminal too early; the taxonomy needs a test per class and a documented escape hatch.

options.label: Retry every error to maxAttempts
options.description: ✅ No taxonomy to maintain; one rule that can never wrongly declare a recoverable error terminal. ✅ Smallest code path in the shared module. ❌ A validation bug or dead webhook URL retries 8 times over hours before anyone sees it, and receivers get 8 identical failing requests.

questions.question:
D9 — What regression contract protects the processWebhookJob() rewrite?
Project/branch/task: main branch, "Plan: Add background job retry framework" (PLAN.md:16-18), Test review. The plan rewrites an existing flow with zero regression coverage; the IRON RULE says this is how to cover it, not whether.
ELI10: You are rewriting the code that sends webhooks to customers. Some behavior must stay identical (the request body, headers, signature on a successful send), and some changes on purpose (retries, a new delivery-id header, dead-letter). A regression contract writes both lists down as tests, so the rewrite cannot quietly break the first list while adding the second.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Without the full contract, a subtle body or signature change ships and every customer's signature verification starts failing; or a timeout retries but the delivery id differs and receivers cannot dedupe. Existing test coverage for this flow could not be graded: the code is not in this repo.
Recommendation: A because six assertions cost minutes with CC, and the one E2E case (worker restart during backoff) is the only thing that actually proves the D4 persistence claim.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10
Net: the whole contract, including the failure paths that motivated this change, vs. the two easy ones. (human: A ~1.5 days / CC: ~25 min; B ~half day / CC: ~8 min)

options.label: Full contract, 6 assertions (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Preserves: success path sends exactly one request with identical body, headers and signature; same X-Delivery-Id on every attempt. ✅ Proves intended changes: 4xx sends once then dead-letters; timeout/5xx retries with the same id; maxAttempts exhausted dead-letters; worker restart mid-backoff still fires the retry [→E2E]. ❌ One E2E test needs a real queue backend in CI, which may be new infrastructure for this project.

options.label: Happy path + delivery id only
options.description: ✅ Catches the highest-blast-radius regression: a changed body or signature on the success path. ✅ Pure unit tests, no queue backend needed in CI. ❌ Retry, dead-letter and restart paths, the entire reason for this change, ship with no proof they behave as approved.

questions.question:
D10 — Cache the dependency graph across retries, and if so where?
Project/branch/task: main branch, "Plan: Add background job retry framework" (PLAN.md:21-23), Performance review.
ELI10: Each retry currently reloads the whole job payload from the database and walks it again to rebuild a dependency graph that did not change since the first attempt. With 8 attempts that is 8x the DB reads and 8x the CPU for a result computed correctly on attempt 1. The plan notes the fix and skips it. The catch with any cache is staleness: if the payload can be edited between attempts, the cached graph must be thrown away. Storing the graph next to the job with a payload version stamp handles that explicitly; a cache in worker memory does not survive restarts and cannot see edits.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Recompute means retry storms during an outage multiply DB load exactly when the DB is already stressed. An in-memory memo serves a stale graph after a payload edit, silently.
Recommendation: A because it removes the redundant work, survives worker restarts (consistent with D4), and makes staleness an explicit, testable branch instead of a hidden one. Cost per recompute is unmeasured here; the win is proportional to attempt count.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=5/10, C=3/10
Net: explicit persisted cache with a version check vs. a fragile process-local memo vs. paying the full cost up to 8 times. (human: A ~1 day / CC: ~15 min; B ~2 hrs / CC: ~5 min)

options.label: Persist graph with job, version-keyed (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Attempt 1 stores the serialized graph plus a payloadVersion (updatedAt or hash); retries skip fetch-and-iterate when versions match. ✅ Survives worker restarts and makes staleness an explicit tested branch: version mismatch recomputes. ❌ Adds a serialized column/field to the job record and a version stamp the payload writer must maintain.

options.label: In-process memo keyed by job id
options.description: ✅ No schema change; a Map in the worker process. ✅ Fast when the retry lands on the same process quickly. ❌ Lost on restart and blind to payload edits between attempts, so it can serve a stale graph with no signal.

options.label: Recompute every attempt (as planned)
options.description: ✅ Always fresh; no cache invalidation to get wrong. ✅ Zero additional code or schema. ❌ Up to 8x the DB reads and graph walks per job, concentrated during outages when retries spike and the DB is already under load.

questions.question:
D11 — TODO: dead-letter operations (retention, alert routing, owner)?
Project/branch/task: main branch, "Plan: Add background job retry framework"; final planning decisions, one TODO candidate.
ELI10: We approved sending terminal failures to a dead-letter set with an alert log (D6.1). That creates an operational surface the plan does not cover: who watches it, where the alert actually goes (log line vs. pager/Slack), how big the set may grow during a long outage, and when old entries are purged. Unwatched dead-letter sets turn into graveyards; that is the known failure mode of the option we chose.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Skipping it means the dead-letter safety net exists but nobody is looking; building it now widens this change beyond retries.
Recommendation: A because it is real follow-up work created by this plan, but it is operations tooling, not part of the retry change itself.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
What: Define dead-letter retention (TTL / max size), route the terminal-failure alert to the on-call channel, name an owner, add a replay runbook. Why: D6.1 dead-letter is only useful if someone acts on it. Context: retry module emits an alert-level log on terminal failure; the queue's failed set holds payload + error; no retention or routing exists. Effort: M. Priority: P2. Depends on: this retry change shipping.
Net: capture the follow-up with its reasoning vs. drop it vs. grow this PR. (TODOS.md does not exist yet; A creates it after plan mode exits.)

options.label: Add to TODOS.md (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Captures the operational gap with motivation, current state and a starting point while it is fresh. ✅ Keeps this PR scoped to retries; ops tooling lands as its own change. ❌ Creates a new TODOS.md file in the repo (written after plan mode exits) that someone must actually pick up.

options.label: Skip, not valuable enough
options.description: ✅ No new file, no backlog entry to maintain. ✅ The alert-level log line from D6.1 still exists as a minimal signal. ❌ The dead-letter set has no owner, retention or routing; the graveyard failure mode is left to chance.

options.label: Build it now in this PR
options.description: ✅ Dead-letter ships fully operable: retention, routed alert, runbook on day one. ✅ No follow-up to track. ❌ Widens this change into alerting integration and retention jobs (human: ~2 days / CC: ~30 min) and delays the retry work.

# Eng review: Plan — Add background job retry framework

Reviewed target: `PLAN.md` on branch `main` (commit 60a0aaf), via `/plan-eng-review`.
Evidence note: this repository contains only `PLAN.md` and `CLAUDE.md`. The 5 worker
files, the job library, and `processWebhookJob()` referenced by the plan are not present,
so every finding is graded against plan text; runtime evidence is **unknown** throughout.
Web research was unavailable (no Aside, no WebSearch) — in-distribution knowledge only.

## Context

The plan adds retry-with-exponential-backoff to background jobs. As written it takes
four shortcuts: a hand-rolled scheduler per worker instead of the job library's retry
hooks, copy-pasted retry envelopes across 5 workers, no regression test for the
`processWebhookJob()` rewrite (which silently changes the delivery guarantee), and a full
payload re-fetch plus dependency-graph recompute on every retry. This review decides,
one choice at a time, which of those to keep and which to fix before implementation.

## Original plan (verbatim, PLAN.md:3-23)

```
# Plan: Add background job retry framework

## Architecture
We'll roll a custom exponential-backoff scheduler inline in each worker
rather than use the existing job library's built-in retry hooks. Same
shape as the library version, but we want full control over the curve.

## Code quality
The retry envelope (compute delay, log attempt, dispatch) is duplicated
across 5 worker files with copy-pasted bodies. We will leave the
duplication for now and refactor "later."

## Tests
The existing `processWebhookJob()` flow gets rewritten as part of this
change. No regression test for the prior at-most-once delivery guarantee
is planned.

## Performance
On every retry we re-fetch the full job payload from the database, then
iterate the payload to recompute the dependency graph. Could cache the
graph on the first attempt; not planned.
```

## Step 0: Scope Challenge

1. **Existing code that already solves a sub-problem:** the job library's built-in retry
   hooks (PLAN.md:7-8: "rather than use the existing job library's built-in retry hooks").
   The plan acknowledges the built-in and rebuilds it. Every mainstream job library exposes
   a custom-backoff hook (BullMQ `backoff.type: 'custom'` + `backoffStrategy`, Sidekiq
   `sidekiq_retry_in`, Celery `retry(countdown=...)`/`retry_backoff`, Oban `backoff/1`,
   Resque/GoodJob equivalents), so "full control over the curve" does not require owning
   the scheduler. **[Layer 1]** reuse candidate. Library identity unverifiable here.
2. **Minimum change set:** one shared backoff function + one hook registration per worker
   (or one shared job base) achieves the stated goal. Inline schedulers in 5 workers is
   scope creep by duplication, not by feature.
3. **Complexity check:** 5 files touched, 0 new classes/services. Below the 8-file / 2-class
   gate; no complexity stop required. The smell is repetition, handled in Code Quality.
4. **Search check:** unavailable this run (see evidence note). Graded from knowledge of the
   named library class only.
5. **TODOS.md:** does not exist in this repo. Nothing blocking; nothing to bundle.
6. **Completeness check:** the plan is a shortcut on three axes (duplication, no regression
   test, no graph cache). Each is minutes of CC work; each is flagged below.
7. **Distribution check:** no new artifact (no CLI/library/container). N/A.

### Scope Challenge findings

- **S1 [P1] (confidence: 8/10) PLAN.md:6-8** — Rolls a custom inline scheduler where the
  job library's retry hooks already exist. Quote: "We'll roll a custom exponential-backoff
  scheduler inline in each worker rather than use the existing job library's built-in retry
  hooks." Inline in-process scheduling also loses pending retries on worker restart/deploy
  unless the plan persists them, which it does not mention; library hooks persist retry
  state in the queue for free. Disposition: **pending → D4**.
- **S2 [P2] (confidence: 9/10) PLAN.md (whole)** — No retry policy bounds are specified:
  max attempts, delay cap, jitter, or terminal handling (dead-letter / permanent failure).
  "Exponential backoff" with none of these is unbounded. Disposition: pending → Architecture
  (D6.x).
- **S3 [P2] (confidence: 9/10) PLAN.md:11-13 / :16-18 / :21-23** — Three declared shortcuts
  ("refactor later", "no regression test", "not planned") that cost minutes with CC. Each is
  taken through its own decision in Sections 2–4.

## Decision ledger

### R1: Retry scheduler ownership — library hooks vs. custom inline scheduler
Finding: S1, P1, confidence 8/10, PLAN.md:6-8, reviewer: plan-eng-review (native)
Plan baseline: custom exponential-backoff scheduler inline in each of 5 workers (original proposal, PLAN.md:6-8)
Runtime evidence: unknown — job library and worker files not in this repository
State: pending

D4 — Retry mechanism: use the job library's built-in retry hooks, or roll the custom inline scheduler?
Project/branch/task: fixture repo on `main`; PLAN.md "Add background job retry framework", finding S1 (PLAN.md:6-8).
ELI10: Your job library already knows how to retry a failed job later. The plan says it will ignore that and write its own "wait, then try again" timer inside each of 5 workers, because you want control over how long the waits are. But almost every job library lets you hand it your own wait-time function, so you get the exact curve you want while the library handles the hard parts: persisting the retry across a process crash, not double-running a job when two workers race, and reporting attempt counts. A hand-rolled inline timer typically loses all three the first time a worker restarts mid-backoff.
Stakes if we pick wrong: with the custom scheduler, a worker restart during a backoff sleep silently drops the retry (job lost) or re-enqueues it twice; with library hooks you inherit its persistence and visibility.
Recommendation: A because it is [Layer 1] proven code, gives the identical control over the curve via one backoff function, and shrinks the change from 5 inline schedulers to one function plus config. Effort: A (human: ~half day / CC: ~10 min), B (human: ~3 days / CC: ~45 min), C (human: ~1 hr / CC: ~5 min).
Completeness: A=9/10, B=5/10, C=N/A (investigation only, approves nothing)
Net: same curve either way; A gets crash-safe persistence and observability for free, B pays for those later or ships without them. Runtime evidence unknown: this repo has no code, so A assumes the library's hook accepts a custom function (true for BullMQ, Sidekiq, Celery, Oban, Que, Faktory).

options.label: A) Library retry hooks + one custom backoff function (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Full control over the curve via a single backoff(attempt) function passed to the library
✅ Retry state persisted by the library: survives worker restarts, no double-run on race
✅ Attempt counts, failure reasons and dead-letter show up in the library's existing tooling
❌ Bound to the library's hook signature; if it lacks per-job backoff functions you need option C first

options.label: B) Custom inline scheduler in each worker (as planned)
options.description:
✅ Zero dependency on the library's retry API; you own every line of the behavior
✅ Can express curves a library hook might not (e.g. per-tenant curves) without a wrapper
❌ Must reimplement persistence, crash-safety, attempt tracking and observability in 5 places
❌ Sleep-in-process backoff loses the retry on any restart or deploy mid-wait

options.label: C) Investigate the library's retry hook API before deciding
options.description:
✅ Removes the one assumption in A: that the hook accepts a custom backoff function
✅ Cheap: read the library's retry docs and one existing worker's config (CC: ~5 min)
❌ Delays the decision; R2-R5 stay pending until this resolves
❌ Approves nothing; the plan keeps the custom scheduler as baseline until you answer again
